summary: Models served from your own Databricks workspace over its OpenAI-compatible surface. The usual choice for the `confidential` tier: the endpoint is inside a boundary you control.

requires.name: databricks
requires.description: The Databricks CLI. Required only for the OAuth credential path; a PAT in DATABRICKS_TOKEN works without it.

requires.name: jq
requires.description: Used by config/bin/dbx-token-cached to read the CLI's JSON token output.
requires.howTo: Any package manager. Only needed on the OAuth path.

requires.name: DATABRICKS_TOKEN
requires.description: A workspace personal access token. The two-minute path: set this and neither the CLI nor jq is needed.
requires.howTo: Workspace -> Settings -> Developer -> Access tokens. Put it in ~/.pi/secrets.env as DATABRICKS_TOKEN=... (chmod 600).

requires.name: DATABRICKS_HOST
requires.description: https://<your-workspace-host>. Read by the Databricks CLI and by config/bin/dbx-token-cached; NOT read by PI (baseUrl is not variable-expanded).
requires.howTo: The installer writes it into config/shell/pi-env.sh from the workspaceHost answer below.

prompts.label: Databricks workspace host, without the scheme
prompts.help: The hostname from your workspace URL. PI does NOT expand $VAR or !cmd inside baseUrl, so this is substituted literally at install time - it cannot be an environment variable.

validate.message: hostname only - no https://, no path, no trailing slash

prompts.label: How should the harness get a Databricks token?

choices.label: OAuth via the Databricks CLI, cached by config/bin/dbx-token-cached (recommended)

prompts.label: Serving-endpoint name for your main / confidential model
prompts.help: Model ids on Databricks are the SERVING-ENDPOINT NAMES in your own workspace. They are per-workspace and nobody can guess them. Discover them with: databricks serving-endpoints list --output json | jq -r '.[].name'

prompts.help: Not the model's advertised window - what your endpoint accepts. Under-declaring is safe; over-declaring makes compaction fire too late.

notes: THE ALL-NULL thinkingLevelMap IS DELIBERATE, AND IT IS NOT A CLAIM THAT YOUR ENDPOINT CANNOT THINK. It says only that no reasoning level is STEERABLE through this provider: `compat.supportsReasoningEffort` is false, so PI never emits `reasoning_effort` on this surface at all, and a model that declares no map at all is read by pi-ai as supporting off/minimal/low/medium/high - five levels that would be offered in the model menu and reach the wire as nothing. All-null is the honest statement of the same wire, and it makes any requested level clamp to `off`, which the emitter turns into no parameter. If your endpoint does accept `reasoning_effort` (an OSS/harmony-style endpoint typically does, and enumerates its own vocabulary in the 400 it returns for a junk value), give that model its own `compat: {"supportsReasoningEffort": true}` plus a map naming the levels it listed, and leave `off` absent so nothing is sent when thinking is off.

THERE IS NO BUILT-IN `databricks` PROVIDER IN PI. This works because Model Serving exposes an OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions surface at https://<host>/serving-endpoints. There is no Responses surface, which is why `api` is `openai-completions` and not left to default.

MODEL IDS ARE SERVING-ENDPOINT NAMES, AND THEY ARE PER-WORKSPACE. `databricks serving-endpoints list --output json | jq -r '.[].name'` is the only way to learn them. Do not copy ids out of anyone else's config - including the examples above, which are illustrative names, not guaranteed to exist anywhere. `id` is the endpoint name on the wire; `name` is only the human label shown in /model.

ADDING MORE MODELS. Append another object to `providers.databricks.models` in config/models.json with the endpoint name as `id`. Databricks-specific request extras (usage_context, AI Gateway guardrail hints) go in that model's `samplingParams`, which is merged verbatim into the request body, or in `headers`.

WHY apiKey IS A CACHED WRAPPER AND NOT `!databricks auth token`. PI re-executes an `!command` credential on EVERY request, with no TTL of its own. An unwrapped CLI call is therefore one OAuth round trip per LLM call. config/bin/dbx-token-cached puts a TTL cache (0600 file in a 0700 dir) in front of it, which turns that into a file read. `$HOME` is expanded by the shell that runs the command, so the reference stays user-agnostic.

COMPAT FLAGS ARE MEASURED, NOT GUESSED. supportsDeveloperRole:false - the foundation-model API rejects the `developer` role with a 400 on every request. supportsReasoningEffort:false - it ignores or rejects reasoning_effort. maxTokensField:max_tokens - it expects the legacy field and 400s on max_completion_tokens. supportsUsageInStreaming:true and supportsFinishReason:true were both verified against a live endpoint. supportsFinishReason is the one whose absence looks like a hung agent rather than an error: if a turn never ends, flip it to false so PI infers the stop itself.

TWO FLAGS DELIBERATELY LEFT UNSET. supportsStrictMode - tool calling works but strict JSON-schema mode is rejected, so expect occasional malformed tool JSON (a model-quality problem, not a config one). cacheControlFormat - Claude-on-Databricks does not surface cache_control breakpoints, and declaring "anthropic" here would report prompt-cache savings that do not exist.

EGRESS CLASS IS `confidential` BECAUSE THE WORKSPACE IS YOURS. That is a DECLARATION about where the data goes, not a network control - nothing in this harness can stop a request reaching a public provider if a tier is bound to one. It is what lets the dispatcher refuse to send a confidential session to a public-class provider by name.

AN IP ACCESS LIST ON THE WORKSPACE LOOKS LIKE AN AUTH FAILURE AND IS NOT ONE. If the workspace denies your current address, every call including inference returns 403 with a body that reads like a credential problem. Check your network position before regenerating tokens.

A ZERO ON THE STATUS LINE MEANS UNPRICED HERE, NOT FREE. Model Serving bills by DBU consumption per endpoint rather than per token, so there is no per-token rate to write into a `cost` object at all, and any number put here would be a conversion this repository invented. `cost` is optional in this file and required on PI's runtime model type, and the provider composer substitutes {input:0,output:0,cacheRead:0,cacheWrite:0} rather than refusing - so sessions on this provider display a flat 0.000 spend while really costing money. Track it in the Databricks account console, not in PI. If you do decide to put an estimate in, the units are DOLLARS PER MILLION TOKENS: PI divides each rate by 1000000 before multiplying by the usage counter.
